Agregar tais resultados em um único estudo é útil para professores interessados em adotar algum aspecto da gamificação em suas aulas, auxiliando-os na decisão sobre quais elementos adotar, ou evitar, levando em consideração o que se deseja alcançar com o uso da gamificação no ambiente de ensino. Os resultados até o momento podem direcionar para as lacunas existentes na gamificação e seu processo, permitindo compreender o que é comumente usado para sair do padrão e gerar inovações.

## AMEAÇAS À VALIDADE

Este estudo adotou um protocolo sólido [13] para mitigar ameaças à validade. Três pesquisadores conduziram todas as fases, obtendo resultados consistentes após resolverem dúvidas em reuniões de grupo. Uma ameaça foi a quantidade limitada de artigos para responder às QPs, levando a discussões com base em um número reduzido deles. Além disso, alguns trabalhos abordavam gamificação em ES de forma não específica. Para trazer transparência, no texto foram destacados os artigos relevantes para cada questão. Outra ameaça foi o escopo dos estudos secundários incluídos, que poderia levar a um viés em direção a áreas específicas. Por exemplo, um artigo específico da área de teste de software [5] pode ter afetado os resultados sobre gamificação em teste e qualidade de software.

## CONCLUSÃO

A gamificação tem sido utilizada por diversos educadores com o intuito de melhorar o processo de ensino e aprendizado.Diante disso, este trabalho teve como objetivo investigar o uso da gamificação no ensino de disciplinas da Engenharia de Software (ES). Para isso foi realizado um estudo terciário, visto que, já existiam estudos secundários recentes que abordavam tal tópico.

Os resultados mostram que a gamificação tem sido utilizada em seus dois formatos (de conteúdo e estrutural, tanto em conjunto quanto separadamente. No entanto, a gamificação estrutural é usada na maioria dos trabalhos. Além disso, é possível afirmar que um dos principais benefícios gerados pela gamificação nos trabalhos analisados é o engajamento e a motivação dos estudantes. A gamificação também pode agir diretamente na melhoria de desempenho, incentivo de boas práticas e estímulo à colaboração, trabalho em equipe e liderança. Com relação aos aspectos negativos, se a gamificação não for planejada e aplicada da forma correta ela pode causar efeitos desmotivadores, e perda de desempenho dos estudantes.

## Personal Variables  

## Results on Personal Characteristics  

In studies on the effects of personal characteristics; it was observed that traits such as extraversion, conscientiousness, determination, and responsibility had an effect on individuals' gamification perceptions and performances [3, 34, 95]. In studies conducted by gender [2, 10, 34, 61, 95, 106], it has been stated that gender can have an effective effect on individuals' perceptions of game elements. In addition, it was also revealed that gender had an effect on students' engagement in the gamified learning environment. In these studies, it was concluded that the effects of game elements are highly personal and may vary greatly between different students.  

## DISCUSSIONS AND CONCLUSION  

Examining the data reveals that there is a misunderstanding between the terms "gamification" and "game- based learning." Actually, there's a considerable distinction between gamification and game- based learning. While game- based learning aims to provide education through games, gamification does not take on the role of learning. Rather, it emphasizes conducting an entertaining learning process with game elements, increasing student motivation and participation, and overcoming obstacles that arise from time to time. In most of the studies examined, the researchers emphasized the use of game elements in non- game contexts and included features such as motivation, facilitating learning, problem solving, and active participation in their definitions. As a result, when we consider the common features of the definitions, we can define it as the use of fun game elements in non- game contexts that enables students to be active in order to increase learning motivation, student participation, and student performance.  

In the articles we examined for our study, Self- Determination Theory was the most frequently used; followed by Flow Theory and Werbach and Hunter's Model. On the other hand, the results of this study showed that no model or theory was used in \(61\%\) of the studies. This finding reveals that the theoretical framework of the studies in the field is not based on a strong foundation. Studies in the literature have indicated that the theory has not been empirically examined and applied, as most studies do not refer to any theory, and this creates an important gap that limits the growth of the field as a whole (Huang et al., 2019; Krath et al., 2021; Nacke & Deterding, 2017; Seaborn & Fels, 2015; Zainuddin et al., 2020). In their literature analysis on gamification in education, Zainuddin et al. (2020), Kalogiannakis et al. (2021), and Nadi- Ravandi and Batooli (2022) found that the majority of the studies lacked a theoretical foundation. The findings of this research indicate that the studies primarily relied on theories and models for the development of gamified learning environments. As Sen (2019) stated in his study, motivation and design- based theories have been used more heavily in recent years. However, Park et al. (2019) and Sanchez et al. (2020) emphasized that the theory- based design of gamified learning systems is not given enough attention....

Gami cation mechanics are essential for the gami ed experience. It is the mechanics that decide which the key parties are, the interactions between them, what the winning conditions are and lastly the time and place for the experience. The interdependent relationship between mechanics, dynamics and emotions will together be used to achieve the desired goal for the company. Mechanics alone are not enough to create an experience that will be useful for the intended purpose, it just creates the structure where the gami ed experience is included.

#### 2.4.2 Dynamics

Gami cation dynamics discloses the behaviour of players when they participate in the experience. Dynamics describe how players follow the mechanics chosen by designers and does not include how the mechanics are actually set. If both the mechanic and dynamic perspectives are derived from the card game Poker it is clear how they differ. The mechanics of Poker

include shut ing, trick-taking and betting while the dynamics is more like bluf ng, cheating, conspiring and bragging. Mechanics like team-based player structures can in gami cation lead to corporation dynamics while individual structures can induce more competitive dynamics. Dynamics of gami cation can be hard to predict, which can lead to unexpected outcomes of both positive and negative nature. The challenge for the designers is to anticipate the dynamics that are emerged from the mechanics of the experience.

#### 2.4.3 Emotions

Gami cation emotions are evoked by individuals that take part in gami ed experiences. Emotions are the results from how users follow mechanics and accordingly generating dynamics. With the same principle as in games the gami ed experience should be both appealing and fun not only on a pragmatic level but also on an emotional level. Assuming that the application usage is purely based on player enjoyment it is considered the most important goal for player engagement in gami cation. Enjoyments can be expressed in positive emotions like excitement, amusement, amazement, surprise, wonder and personal triumph. To have fun is an important aspect in gami ed environments, it is also connected with different types of emotions. It doesn't always have to be positive emotions but also emotions like disappointment or sadness.

Figure 2.1 illustrates the interdependent relationship between mechanics, dynamics and emotions. Depending on how these principles are being used there are possibilities to extend the player's experience. Different experiences can be generated when making small changes in one of the principles that effect the other two. The MDE framework facilitates the perception of gami ed experience dependent on players and designers. The focus is different depending on who you are. For example, different types of challenges and the associated dynamics that comes with it are more important for the players than the rules that the designer has set to make it possible. To understand the role of these three different principles and their internal relationship are the key for creating successful gami ed experiences.[38]

results.summary:
According to self‐determination theory (Ryan & Deci, [44]), students' intrinsic motivation depends on the satisfaction of three inherent psychological needs (autonomy, competence and relatedness). Gamification has aroused criticism for its potential negative effects on student learning and intrinsic motivation. Some researchers have argued that game design elements (eg, points, badges and a leader board) are typical extrinsic motivators that can only facilitate extrinsic motivation (eg, Hanus & Fox, [22]; Mekler et al., [37]). We argue that the effect of gamification on human motivation is essentially two sides of the same coin. It can enhance students' intrinsic motivation and provide extrinsic motivation (Buckley & Doyle, [5]).

In our study, we inferred from the interview responses that gamification provides intrinsic motivation, in particular, it satisfies the three basic psychological needs that motivate self‐initiated behaviour: autonomy, relatedness and competence. Regarding the need for autonomy, the students indicated in the interviews that the leader board in the mixed gamification condition helped them self‐regulate their learning. They were able to monitor their team and other teams' progress and seek help from others (need for relatedness). Students' need for competence has also been fulfilled because gamification can provide immediate positive feedback on their good performance or behaviours. On the other hand, our study also reported how game elements had affected students' extrinsic motivation in learning. In the interviews, the students were reported as eager to win success and use whatever means to get the awards. As a result, it caused plagiarism among students. This phenomenon was considered as external motivation affected by reward and competition.

Meanwhile, not all extrinsic motivation is negative. For example, Li ([32]) developed a scaffold‐based gamification pedagogy and examined its effects on students' reading abilities, motivation and interest through a gamified reading platform Reading Battle. She found that the motivation and interest of active users of Reading Battle were enhanced. Interestingly, this scaffold‐based gamification pedagogy internalised students' extrinsic motivation for reading, and the effects persisted even after the students stopped using Reading Battle. Therefore, a good gamification design should be highlighted to facilitate the internalisation of extrinsic motivation (such as through perceived personal value; Mitchell et al., [38]).

### CONCLUSION, LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

This study makes important contributions to the gamification literature. Specifically, it is the first attempt to explore the innovative designs of mixed and non‐digital gamification and their relevant effectiveness. Although gamification has been implemented in blended learning environments (eg, Huang et al., 2018), to the best of our knowledge, no studies have combined digital and non‐digital game design elements to form a mixed gamification and improve the blended learning effectiveness. The quantitative results of this study indicate that both gamification approaches lead to similar improvements in reading outcomes. Although non‐digital gamification improves course satisfaction, we should not ignore the unique affordances of digital gamification in providing timely and accurate reflections of student performance or its influence on cognitive engagement. The qualitative results helped identify factors that potentially drove the quantitative results. As such, our findings may help to improve the quality of mixed and non‐digital gamification designs.

Nevertheless, this study has several limitations. First, this study collected data from junior secondary grade students, which may not represent other student populations. Future studies with primary grade or university students could ascertain whether the findings hold true for lower or higher grades. Second, we did not use a leader board in the non‐digital gamification condition due to the difficulty in recording students' points manually. The effective design of non‐digital gamification deserves more study, including introducing non‐digital leader boards in classrooms and more attractive non‐digital game design elements. Given that some students in the mixed gamification condition expressed dissatisfaction with the difficulty of climbing up the leader board, future studies could examine resetting the leader board to zero after each session, having different ranks of leader boards or having leader boards assessing students' different knowledge. Third, although our qualitative data allowed us to examine students' course satisfaction in‐depth, we only used one item in the questionnaire to measure students' overall course satisfaction. Future studies could address this limitation by adding more items in the questionnaire, such as evaluating students' satisfaction with the teaching methods, knowledge they acquired and overall learning experience (Orús et al., [39]).

# Gamification is not Working: Why?

## 摘要

Gamification is a trending topic in the scientific community. It is the art of incorporating game elements and game design principles into non-game context. The phenomenon has garnered tremendous attention especially in the field of education and academics. Yet, since it appeared a decade ago, its ascension both in education and other domains hasn’t been uniform, with several failed and inconclusive results. Consequently, scholars have, over the years, made several efforts to probe why gamification isn’t succeeding as hoped. We attempt, therefore, to contribute to this effort by reviewing and discussing some of the core reasons why gamification seems to be faltering in the field of learning and education. Our findings revealed four (4) factors why gamification could be failing. Shallow gamification which is the simplistic and surficial application of game elements on a learning system or activity without transforming the core experience is one determinant. Overjustification effect, the excessive and arbitral use of rewards (extrinsic motivators), which hampers intrinsic motivation is another success determinant. The ‘badges, points, and leaderboards (BPL) gamification’ (or BPL triad) which refers to the use of basic game elements such as the badges, points, and leaderboards is also one reason gamification is still struggling. Lastly, the overreliance on narrow models and theories to explain or design gamified experiences is identified as a factor for gamification haziness. Our study suggests several antidotes to these highlighted challenges, such as deep intentional designs that transcend surface-level implementation of game elements (what is called ‘deep gamification’). Amidst the spree of excessive extrinsic rewards anyhow, we propose a careful consideration of implementing reward-based game elements, especially in multiple learning settings. Again, a move-away from the narrow and overly used models such as the self-determination theory, and flow theory could open success pathways. As we believe, narrow theoretical lens through which gamification is often viewed serves as a limiting factor, impeding the field's progression and obscuring the full potential of gamification as an approach.

# GAMIFICATION: THE NEGATIVE IMPACT OF GAMIFICATION IN EDUCATIONAL CONTEXT FROM STUDENT’S PERSPECTIVE

Akbar, Sulaiman (2024) GAMIFICATION: THE NEGATIVE IMPACT OF GAMIFICATION IN EDUCATIONAL CONTEXT FROM STUDENT’S PERSPECTIVE. Undergraduate thesis, Universitas Muhammadiyah Malang.
...
## Abstract

Gamification is a method of learning involving game features like leaderboards, points, badges, levels, and time limits into non-gaming situations with the intention of making learning activities more enjoyable. The goal of gamification is to raise student confidence, motivation, and performance when completing assignments. The purpose of this research is to identify gamification's disadvantages. "What are the negative impacts of gamification in educational contexts from the student's perspective?" is the research question of this study. Both open-ended and closed-ended questions are used in questionnaire for this study. According to the study's findings, there are nine disadvantages by employing gamification in educational settings. Students expressed dissatisfaction with game features in gamification. Students also struggled to adjust and lack confidence when using gamification due to unfamiliar game features. In specifics, gamification has the potential to demotivate and annoy students, as well as make them feel hopeless.
